title: Janhvi Kapoor Is About to Walk Into a Monster Movie. The Director Made Tumbbad.
excerpt: After the Peddi storm, the actress is pivoting hard — signing on for a large-scale creature horror spectacle with Rahi Anil Barve that could rewrite her entire filmography.
body:
Here is what nobody expected from Janhvi Kapoor's 2026: a pivot into creature horror. Not a cute haunted-house comedy. Not a jumpscare anthology. A full-blown, large-scale, Jio Studios-backed creature horror film directed by the man who made Tumbbad — arguably the most visually stunning and emotionally devastating horror film Indian cinema has ever produced.

According to an exclusive Pinkvilla report, Janhvi is in advanced talks with director Rahi Anil Barve for a project that would take her into territory no mainstream Bollywood actress has ever seriously explored. The paperwork isn't signed yet, but insiders say she's shown "keen interest" and is expected to lock it in soon.

If she does, it won't just be a career move. It'll be a statement.

Why This Pairing Makes Everyone Pay Attention

Let's talk about what Rahi Anil Barve actually did with Tumbbad. In 2018, he released a film that took twelve years to make, looked like a Guillermo del Toro fever dream set in the Konkan, and told a story about generational greed through the lens of a rain-soaked, tentacle-armed mythological creature. It earned a modest ₹13 crore on its initial run — then became a genuine cult phenomenon. When it was re-released in 2024, it earned over ₹30 crore more, becoming one of Indian cinema's most extraordinary second-life stories.

Now imagine that filmmaker — that eye, that patience, that willingness to build entire worlds from scratch — working with a proper studio budget from Jio Studios and a leading lady with one of the biggest social media followings in Indian cinema.

"It's a never-done-before role for Janhvi and one that demands extensive preparation. She is expected to sign the dotted lines soon. Once the paperwork is completed, the actress will undergo intensive acting workshops to get into the skin of the character." — Industry source to Pinkvilla

The Character Sounds Intense

Details are still tightly guarded, but what's leaked so far suggests this isn't a role where Janhvi shows up, looks gorgeous, and screams at the right moments. The character reportedly demands extensive emotional and psychological preparation — the kind of deep-dive method work that changes how an actor carries themselves on screen.

The production team is already planning detailed workshops and character-building sessions before cameras roll. If the Tumbbad approach is any indicator, Barve's prep process is meticulous and immersive. He doesn't direct actors so much as pull them into the world he's been building in his head for years.

For Janhvi, who has been steadily building her range from the tenderness of Dhadak to the commercial spectacle of Peddi — and who's been navigating a very public controversy around that film's leaked chats — this could be the role that forces critics to take her seriously as a performer, not just a star kid with great Instagram numbers.

The State of Horror in Bollywood

Here's the thing about Indian horror: it's almost always played for laughs. Stree, Bhool Bhulaiyaa, Bhooth Bangla — these are comedies with spooky set dressing, and they work brilliantly. But genuine, atmospheric, visually ambitious horror? That lane is almost entirely empty in mainstream Hindi cinema.

Tumbbad was the exception. And the fact that its re-release outperformed its original run proved there's a massive audience hungry for horror that treats them like adults — that builds dread instead of punchlines, that uses creature design as art rather than a jump-scare gimmick.

A Jio Studios-backed creature horror with Barve at the helm and Janhvi as the face represents the best chance Bollywood has at creating something genuinely new in the genre. Not a franchise play. Not a comedy hybrid. A proper, ambitious, dark horror spectacle.

What the Diaspora Should Watch For

For audiences in the US, UK, and Canada who've been streaming Tumbbad on repeat (it's on Prime Video — go watch it if you somehow haven't), this project is a reason to get excited. Indian horror has historically been dismissed by Western audiences, but Tumbbad crossed that barrier. A spiritual successor with bigger ambitions and a marquee star could do what no Indian horror film has done: open theatrically in diaspora markets as an event, not an afterthought.

Moreover, the film's exploration of themes like generational trauma and cultural mythology may resonate deeply with NRIs, who often grapple with their own identities and family histories. This connection could lead to increased interest in Indian cinema among diaspora audiences, potentially boosting remittances as they seek to support films that reflect their experiences.

Production is expected to begin later this year, though no release date has been announced. Given Barve's famously painstaking process, don't expect this one to rush. The man took twelve years on Tumbbad. He's not going to phone this one in.

But when it arrives — whenever it arrives — the combination of Barve's vision and Janhvi's willingness to step completely outside her comfort zone could produce something Indian cinema hasn't seen before.

And honestly? That's more exciting than another rom-com.
